manako.blurb: A retired chemist in a tea house

settled.text: The old man who owns the tea house is Manako, and he gives his name freely.
Manako was a chemist for the Directorate, decades ago, and as a junior he was sent on the same errand the party gets.
He came back from that errand empty-handed and was laughed at, and he has spent years going over what he should have done.

His plan: take the docket at its word and requisition a replacement vial, a real and expensive part, which needs a countersignature from a desk above the sender's and makes a form saying who asked, and why.
He is the Directorate scientist who had a "breakdown" at a science conference, caused a huge fuss, and was expelled.
Manako's tea house is on The Slope, the hillside district of the city where he has a lot of influence.
Manako founded Cicada. The Directorate has never linked the tea-house owner to the cult, and the party must make both discoveries themselves: that Cicada has an author, and who.
Trainee messages are read: by the Directorate as routine policy, and by the Watcher, which reads what is typed. A player who messages Manako is read too.

section-officer.blurb: Section Officer — the party's immediate superior (Directorate)

settled.text: Section Officer Vetch runs Section Nine. He is never wrong in his own account.
On their first afternoon, Vetch sends Section Nine into the city with a stores docket for COMPOUND, LEVELLING, BUBBLE, ONE (1): the bubble in a spirit level.
At supper on the first day, Vetch reads Section Nine the night's worst job in front of the hall: storm drain clearance under the old town, from Dock C at twenty-one hundred.
At Dock C, Vetch gives them the job in one line: power to the drainage line, clear the compactor feed, report to him when it runs. He waits for them at the top.

When the exercise at the end of Episode Two turns into real combat, Vetch tells Section Nine not to act. They are put where the only sensible or heroic thing to do is act, and they still get in trouble with Vetch for acting.
Vetch sends every new section on a fool's errand because it was done to him, and he believes it builds character. The same was done to Manako, decades ago.
Vetch gives Section Nine the drains because of the vial requisition, or, if they came back empty-handed, for the laugh. He never says so.

open.text: Whether Vetch was ever in a Frame is not decided; whether his pettiness is disappointed ambition or was always this changes how he plays. Nor is it decided whether he appears at all after the party leaves his section.
candidates: he was once a pilot, washed out
he disappears from the story after the promotion
open.decideBy: before the party leaves his section

settled.text: Shucks Mordant is the Directorate's head of medical.
Shucks is the one founder the players meet at once: he runs their medical, and his badge says MORDANT.
Asked about his right hand, Shucks says it wandered off. He means it, and it sounds like a joke.
When Section Nine climb out of the drains, Vetch is holding their vial requisition, countersigned in green ink over Medical's stamp: Rand, Medical. Nobody called Rand works in Medical; he has asked.
Shucks's right hand is a prosthetic. His real right hand, Rand, is a detached familiar loose in the city, and he doesn't know where it is from day to day.
Shucks has the intake forms ask for mothers' maiden names so he can trace the marker through families. Nobody else remembers why the forms ask.

Rand writes in Shucks's own handwriting from before the hand came off. Shucks writes left-handed now, so nobody alive knows that hand, but anything the founders signed two hundred years ago shows it, the charter included.

Rand countersigns Section Nine's vial requisition the night they file it, with Medical's stamp from Shucks's desk and in Shucks's old handwriting, because it enjoys making the rules bite the officer who hazed them. Nobody called Rand works in Medical.
Rand reads everything on Shucks's desk. The night after Intake Medicals it read his notes and found six carriers of the marker in one intake, which it had never seen.

If Section Nine files no requisition, Rand countersigns whatever paper of theirs goes in that night instead: the docket handed back, or the receipt for a vial they bought. On the back of a docket it writes "Received, one (1)."

open.text: Why Shucks has the standing to be let in at once to the Deputy Director's office is not decided; the party sees only that the intake doctor has standing near the top of the building with no visible reason. He must not become their protector whatever the answer.
